title: Unit 5: Regression Analysis

topics.name: Scatterplots and association
covers: Graphical Representations Between Two Quantitative Variables

guide.title: Regression analysis: review guide
guide.intro: This unit describes relationships between two quantitative variables with scatterplots, correlation, and a least-squares regression line. Inference for the slope is not part of the 2026-27 course.

sections.title: Scatterplots
body: Put the explanatory variable on the x-axis and the response on the y-axis. Describe direction, form, strength, and unusual points, in context.
points: An association does not show cause and effect. A lurking variable may affect both variables.

sections.title: Correlation
body: The correlation r measures the direction and strength of a linear association. It is between −1 and 1, has no units, and is not resistant to outliers.
points: r = ±1 means all points lie exactly on a line. r near 0 means a weak linear association (there may still be a curved one).
r² is the fraction of the variation in y accounted for by the linear model with x.

sections.title: Least-squares regression and residuals
body: The least-squares line ŷ = a + bx minimises the sum of squared residuals. Interpret the slope as the predicted change in y for each one-unit increase in x.
points: Residual = actual y − predicted ŷ. A positive residual means the point is above the line.
A residual plot with no pattern suggests a linear model is appropriate. A curve suggests it is not.
Extrapolation (predicting far outside the x-values in the data) is unreliable.

example.prompt: A regression of exam score on hours studied gives ŷ = 52 + 6x. A student studied 4 hours and scored 70. Find the predicted score and the residual.
example.solution: ŷ = 52 + 6(4) = 76. Residual = 70 − 76 = −6: the student scored 6 points below the prediction.

misconceptions: Only a randomized experiment can show cause and effect.
It means no linear relationship. The data might follow a curve.

questions.prompt: A scatterplot shows that students who study more hours tend to have higher test scores. How is this association described?
choices: Positive association
No association
Negative association
Proof that studying causes higher scores
questions.explanation: As one variable increases the other tends to increase, which is a positive association.
choiceExplanations: There is a clear upward trend, so there is an association.
A negative association would show scores falling as hours rise.
An observational association does not prove cause and effect.

questions.prompt: The correlation between two variables is r = −0.9. What does this tell you?
choices: The slope of the regression line is −0.9
90% of the points lie on the regression line
There is a weak negative linear association
There is a strong negative linear association
questions.explanation: |r| = 0.9 is close to 1, so the linear association is strong, and the negative sign means one variable tends to decrease as the other increases.
choiceExplanations: The slope equals r only when the two standard deviations are equal. In general b = r·(s_y/s_x).
r does not count points on the line.
An r of −0.9 is close to −1, which is strong, not weak.

questions.prompt: The regression line is ŷ = 12 + 3x. What is the predicted value of y when x = 5?
choiceExplanations: 17 adds x to the intercept, leaving out the slope.
60 multiplies the intercept by x.
15 adds the intercept and the slope without multiplying the slope by x.

questions.prompt: For the line ŷ = 12 + 3x, a data point has x = 5 and y = 30. What is its residual?
questions.explanation: Predicted ŷ = 27. Residual = actual − predicted = 30 − 27 = 3. The point is 3 units above the line.
choiceExplanations: −3 subtracts in the wrong order. Residual = actual − predicted.
57 adds the actual and predicted values.
27 is the predicted value, not the residual.

questions.prompt: A regression of test score (points) on hours studied gives ŷ = 52 + 6x. How should the slope be interpreted?
choices: For each additional hour studied, the predicted test score increases by 6 points
Studying explains 6% of the variation in scores
A student who studies 0 hours is predicted to score 6 points
Every student's score increases by exactly 6 points for each extra hour
questions.explanation: The slope is the predicted change in the response for a one-unit increase in the explanatory variable.
choiceExplanations: That describes r², not the slope.
The predicted score at 0 hours is the intercept, 52.
The line gives predicted (average) values. Individual students vary around it.

questions.prompt: For a linear regression, r = 0.9. Which statement about r² is correct?
choices: About 81% of the points lie on the regression line
Predictions are correct about 81% of the time
r² = 0.9, the same as r
About 81% of the variation in y is accounted for by the linear model with x
questions.explanation: r² = 0.9² = 0.81, the proportion of the variation in y explained by the linear relationship with x.
choiceExplanations: r² does not count points on the line.
r² measures explained variation, not how often a prediction is exactly right.
r² is r squared: 0.81, not 0.9.

questions.prompt: For two variables, r = 0.6, s_x = 2, and s_y = 10. What is the slope of the least-squares regression line of y on x?
choiceExplanations: 12 multiplies r by both standard deviations instead of by their ratio.
0.12 uses s_x/s_y instead of s_y/s_x.
5 is s_y/s_x without multiplying by r.

questions.prompt: Across many cities, the number of fire trucks and the amount of fire damage have r = 0.7. Which conclusion is most reasonable?
choices: The correlation shows there is no relationship
The association may be explained by a lurking variable such as city size
Fire trucks cause fire damage
Removing fire trucks would reduce fire damage
questions.explanation: This is observational data. Bigger cities tend to have both more fire trucks and more fire damage, so city size can explain the association.
choiceExplanations: r = 0.7 shows a moderately strong positive association.
Correlation in observational data does not show cause and effect.
That is a causal claim the data cannot support.
